newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila's Congo says climate right for investment.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's Congo says climate right for investment.

text.p: The Democratic Republic of the Congo appealed on Tuesday for foreign investment, saying President Laurent Kabila's government was creating a secure climate for business.

Finance Minister Mawampanga Mwana Nanga said in an interview that the former Zaire was looking to foreign investors for its reconstruction plans after economic anarchy in the 32-year rule of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko.
"Conditions are now ripe for foreign investors to come here. We have security, we have a good government. You have macro-economic stability, what else do you ask," Mawampanga said.
Noting that investors were keen on South Africa even while it grappled with internal unrest, Mawapanga said: "I don't see why they would not come here when there is no shooting."
Kabila took power in May after a seven-month bush war and pledged to revamp the ailing economy left by Mobutu, who is battling cancer in Morocco.
"Change is not something you achieve overnight. It's a whole process you go through. We want investors to come and participate in the reconstruction effort.
"We are builders. We are not thieves or people who have come here to make quick and big bucks."
Congo's vast mineral reserves should have made the former Belgian colony one of the potentially wealthiest countries on the continent, but Mobutu left behind foreign debt amounting to $14 billion.

Kabila's government has set up special commissions to audit the hefty internal and external debt as a prelude to talks and then a conference with the country's creditors. It has ruled out debt repayment for the time being.

Major donor countries shunned the former Zaire because of repeated human rights violations and the slow pace of democratic reforms under Mobutu. Some, including the United States, have said aid could be restored if Kabila improves the country's human rights record.
A senior World Bank official said this month that donors were ready to work with Kabila's Congo because its revival was crucial to the fortunes of other states in Central Africa.
A European Union mission announced earlier this month that Brussels was ready to resume cooperation with the ex-Zaire after a five-year freeze amid charges of misrule against Mobutu.
A conference between Kabila's government and donors is scheduled for October, most likely in Paris.

"Preparations (for the meeting) are under way. We are quite advanced. We have broken it into two parts, one (preparatory) meeting will take place on September 6 and the real conference will take place on October 14," Mawampanga said.
"But the issue is for us to jump-start the economy. Everybody knows out there that this country has the potential to face its obligations," the minister said.
He added that the Congolese franc would tbe introduced "soon" to replace the discredited Zaire currency inhertited from the Mobutu era.
Kabila has already awarded contracts for the printing of new banknotes to replace Zaire notes churned out by Mobutu as his crude solution to ex-Zaire's economic problems.
